blocks.text: Disappointed, K. took the letter and put it into his pocket. Even in the most favorable case, the advantage that the recommendation could bring him was comparatively smaller than the harm that lay in the fact that the manufacturer knew of his trial and that the painter was spreading the news further. He could scarcely force himself to thank the manufacturer, who was already on his way to the door, with a few words. "I shall go there," he said, as he took leave of the manufacturer at the door, "or, since I am very busy just now, write to him that he might come to my office sometime." "I knew very well," said the manufacturer, "that you would find the best way out. To be sure, I thought that you would prefer to avoid inviting people like this Titorelli into the bank in order to speak with him here about the trial. Nor is it always advantageous to let letters to such people out of one's hands. But you have no doubt thought everything through and know what you may do." K. nodded and accompanied the manufacturer through the anteroom as well. Yet despite his outward calm, he was greatly alarmed at himself. He had really said that he would write to Titorelli only in order to show the manufacturer somehow that he appreciated the recommendation and was immediately considering the possibilities of meeting with Titorelli, yet if he had regarded Titorelli's assistance as valuable, he would not have hesitated to write to him in earnest either. The dangers, however, that this might entail he had recognized only through the manufacturer's remark. Could he actually rely so little on his own judgment already? If it was possible that he should invite a questionable person into the bank by means of an explicit letter in order to ask him, separated from the Deputy Director by only a door, for advice concerning his trial, was it not then possible and even very probable that he was overlooking other dangers as well, or running straight into them? There was not always someone standing beside him to warn him. And just now, when he meant to act with all his powers collected, such doubts about his own vigilance, hitherto alien to him, had to arise! Were the difficulties that he felt in carrying out his office work now to begin in the trial as well? Now, to be sure, he could no longer comprehend at all how it had been possible for him to have wanted to write to Titorelli and invite him into the bank.

He was still shaking his head over this when the attendant stepped to his side and drew his attention to three gentlemen who were sitting here in the anteroom on a bench. They had already been waiting a long time to be admitted to K. Now that the attendant was speaking with K., they had risen, and each wanted to seize a favorable opportunity to approach K. ahead of the others. Since the bank was so inconsiderate as to let them waste their time here in the waiting room, they too wished to show no further consideration. "Chief Clerk," one of them already said. But K. had had the attendant bring him his winter coat and, while putting it on with the attendant's help, said to all three of them: "Forgive me, gentlemen, unfortunately I have no time at the moment to receive you. I beg your pardon most sincerely, but I have an urgent business errand to attend to and must leave at once. You have seen for yourselves how long I was detained just now. Would you be so kind as to come back tomorrow, or whenever you wish? Or shall we perhaps discuss the matters by telephone? Or would you perhaps like to tell me briefly now what it is about, and I will then give you a detailed written reply. Best of all, however, would be if you came another time." These proposals of K.'s threw the gentlemen, who were now to have waited completely in vain, into such astonishment that they looked at one another in silence. "We are agreed, then?" asked K., who had turned toward the attendant, who was now bringing him his hat as well. Through the open door to K.'s room one could see how heavily the snowfall had increased outside. K. therefore turned up his coat collar and buttoned it high beneath his throat.
